A COUNTEREXAMPLE TO KOUROVKA NOTEBOOK
PROBLEM 16.45
ALEC KRIEBEL
Abstract
Let b(G) be the largest size of an inclusion-minimal base over all permutation representations of a ﬁnite
group G, with bases taken for the permutation image, and let µ0(G) be the largest size of an independent
subset of G. We construct an explicit aﬃne group of order 100920 for which b(G) = 3 < 4 = µ0(G), giving
a negative answer to Kourovka Notebook Problem 16.45. The maximum remains three when restricted
to faithful representations. The proof is structural: every subgroup missing the translation subgroup
has faithful base invariant at most two, and every nontrivial normal subgroup contains the translations.
The independent four-set gives an irredundant intersection family whose intersection is central in the
complement but not normal in the a ﬃne group.
2020 Mathematics subject classiﬁcation: Primary 20B05; Secondary 20D30, 20D60.
Keywords and phrases: Permutation bases, independent sets, ﬁnite groups, subgroup lattices, Kourovka
Notebook.
1. Introduction
A subset S of a ﬁnite group X is independent if x < hS n fxgi for every x 2 S . Write
µ0(X) for the largest size of such a subset; it need not generate X. For an action
ρ : X ! Sym(Ω), a base is a set of points with pointwise stabilizer ker ρ. A base
is minimal if it is inclusion-minimal. Let b(X) be the largest size of a minimal base
over all permutation representations of X, and let bf(X) denote the same maximum
restricted to faithful representations. In particular, b(1) = bf(1) = µ0(1) = 0. The
deﬁnitions allow intransitive and nonfaithful actions. Allowing inﬁnite Ω makes no
diﬀerence: choosing a moved point for each nonidentity element of the ﬁnite image
gives a ﬁnite subbase of every base.
Cameron’s Problem 16.45 in the Kourovka Notebook asks whether b(X) = µ0(X)
for every ﬁnite group X [4]. The inequality b(X)  µ0(X) is known. Cameron uses
b2 for b, and uses µ0 in [ 2] and µ" in [ 3] for our independence invariant. In contrast,
Anagnostopoulou-Merkouri and Burness [ 1, Remark 1(c)] restrict their b2 to faithful
actions, so it corresponds to our bf. The all-actions question is posed in Cameron’s
2024 account [ 3, Section 6, Proposition 2 and the following discussion] and in the
September 2026 notebook. We prove the following.

The proof separates two intersection conditions in the subgroup lattice. Inde-
pendence corresponds to irredundant intersection families with arbitrary intersection,
whereas permutation bases require that intersection to be normal. In our example an
independent four-set gives a family with intersection of order two, central in H but not
normal in G. The faithful upper bound follows by restricting an intersection family
to a subgroup that does not contain the translations. The normal-subgroup structure
then handles every nonfaithful action. No enumeration of the subgroup lattice of G is
required, and no minimum-order assertion is made.

Reproducibility and use of artiﬁcial intelligence
The proof above is independent of subgroup enumeration. A supplementary ver-

the matrix group, compare all its subgroups, and check the a ﬃne witnesses. It also
records a characteristic-eleven example showing why the line-stabilizer hypothesis
matters. The current package is available in the repository snapshot of 25 Septem-
ber 2026 . An earlier version and its original veriﬁcation materials are archived at
doi:10.5281/zenodo.22929486. That version is also hosted in the Kourovka Note-
book’s online repository .
OpenAI Codex (https://openai.com/codex/) was used during 19–25 Septem-

and exact veriﬁcation programs, search and check references, and prepare the sub-

source reviews. Historical application and model build identiﬁers were not consistently
recorded. These checks are not external peer review or proof-assistant certiﬁcation.

4. Reproduction and limits
The README gives ordinary Python and C++17 commands and the
expected outputs. Python uses only its standard library; all mathemati-
cal arithmetic is exact. The reconstruction programs read no precomputed
certiﬁcate. The two supplied implementations and a newly written checker
agree on all 76 subgroups as sets of actual matrices. The two Python im-

element set. Saved expected outputs are used only for subsequent compari-

These programs check explicit ﬁnite claims and provide reproducibility;
they do not replace the structural proof of the universal bounds, establish
bibliographic novelty, or imply external human peer review. The paper and

is claimed.
